summary: L-4 cab reported built 1931 on Sister Rocks; cab now gone, firefinder post reported standing; reached on foot by trail.

facts.status_note: Cab gone; the main center firefinder post was reported still standing.

access.note: Reached on foot from the Observation Peak Trail; the site lies within the Gifford Pinchot National Forest.

visit.trail_note: Leave the Observation Peak Trail and turn onto the Sister Rocks Trail; Willhite lists a hiking distance of 1.6 miles.

events.note: Lookout symbol shown on the 1912 Columbia National Forest map
Panoramic view of the site, captioned 7-12-1934
Registered on the Former Fire Lookout Sites register as US 1342, WA 242

evidence.supports: Two rocky prominences just outside Trapper Creek Wilderness
evidence.quote: The two rocky prominences of Sister Rocks are just outside the Trapper Creek Wilderness and are part of the Sister Rocks Research Natural Area, which was established for the study of climax silver fir forest.

evidence.supports: Site beside the Trapper Creek Wilderness north boundary
evidence.quote: Located at the very north boundary of the Trapper Creek Wilderness Area, access is on fairly long on forest roads but not too rough.
The 1912 Columbia National Forest map shows the lookout symbol there.

evidence.supports: Possibly one of the first lookouts in the area, north of 1902 Yacolt Burn
evidence.quote: With its location just north of the 1902 Yacolt Burn area, it may have been one of the first in the area.
Built in 1931, this L-4 cab is now gone.

evidence.supports: Cab reported built 1931; main center firefinder post still standing
evidence.quote: The L-4 cab was reported as built in 1931 and the main center firefinder post is still standing.

evidence.supports: 1934 panoramic credited to National Archives Pacific Northwest Region
evidence.quote: Sister Rocks Lookout panoramic 7-12-1934 (N) - courtesy of National Archives-Pacific Northwest Region

evidence.supports: Route leaves Observation Peak Trail for Sister Rocks Trail
evidence.quote: After about a mile of trail and steadily climbing, just past the highest point, turn right on the Sister Rocks Trail.

evidence.supports: Route starts on the Observation Peak Trail
evidence.quote: Taking the Observation Peak Trail from the northern most access is the quickest

evidence.supports: Short hike to a rocky viewpoint
evidence.quote: Short hike to a rocky viewpoint over the Trapper Creek Wilderness

evidence.supports: Vertical rusting pipe on higher rock, purpose unknown
evidence.quote: The first, and higher, Sister Rock is distinguished by its vertical rusting pipe (no one seems to know the purpose of this pipe).

evidence.supports: Administered by the U.S. Forest Service

resolved_conflicts.explanation: WillhiteWeb places the site at the very north boundary of Trapper Creek Wilderness; Oregon Hikers says it is just outside the wilderness. The story says it is beside the wilderness, which both allow.

WillhiteWeb lists a 1.6-mile hiking distance; Oregon Hikers lists a 3.9-mile Sister Rocks Easy hike with 750 ft of gain; the pages do not say whether both start from the same trailhead. The story gives only the Willhite figure.

notes_for_editor: Two web searches and six page reads found no staffing history, fire history or reports of when the cab was removed, so the story leaves those out. Access is set to public from the hiking route and Forest Service ownership, not from an explicit access statement. Willhite's 1912 map note and 1931 build date may indicate earlier use of the site than the cab. The story does not resolve that. The brief's access 'unknown' is replaced with public, supported by the route and Forest Service ownership.
